newsitem.title: YEMEN: Suspect in Yemen schools shooting goes on trial.
newsitem.headline: Suspect in Yemen schools shooting goes on trial.

text.p: A man accused of shooting dead three children, a headmistress and a teacher in an attack at two schools went on trial on Monday in a courtroom packed with hundreds of enraged people.

Officials had said earlier that six children were killed in the shooting on Sunday, but the prosecutor general at the trial said only three were dead and the others were in hospital in critical condition.
Mohammad Ahmad Misleh was charged with murdering five people, attempting to murder 12 others and resisting arrest and a verdict was expected later on Monday.

Misleh, sitting in a wheelchair in a steel cage in the packed courtroom, told the three-judge panel that he had meant to kill the husband of the headmistress of Tala'eh school, alleging that the couple had approved the kidnapping and rape of his eight-year-old daughter 18 months ago.
He said the kidnappers, with whom he had a feud over a plot of land, had also received the approval of the administration at the other school, Musa Ibn Naseer, to kidnap his son.
But the prosecutor general produced a medical examiner's report saying the girl was still a virgin and was not raped. There was no independent confirmation of the kidnappings claim.
The girl was brought into the courtroom by the prosecutor. She greeted her father through the steel bars of his cage, but remained silent when the prosecutor asked her questions.
"They told me to say I was insane, but I am not," Misleh, sporting a long, thick beard and wearing a long grey Arab robe, told the judges. He did not say who told him to say that.
The Yemeni man opened fire from an assault rifle on hundreds of students aged between six and 18 as they lined up at the two schools to go into morning classes.
Police arrested the gunman after an exchange of fire with security forces in which he was wounded in the leg as he tried to escape. None of the security forces was reported hurt.

Hundreds of people, including most of the families of the victims, crowded into the courtroom. Thousands others, including students from the two schools and their parents, gathered in the street outside the courthouse under heavy security.
Grim-faced and angry, many said they were shocked by the first such crime in Yemen and called for the death penalty.
"We expect and want a quick sentencing to this ugly crime," said 15-year-old Hamza Ali Ahmed, a student from Tala'eh school.
"We will not have peace of mind until the killer is executed," said Mansour Serhan, 16, from Musa Ibn Naseer school.
Witnesses had described the assailant as a disgruntled former bus driver who had been sacked by the headmistress.

Prosecutor-general Mohammad al-Badri told the official news agency SABA on Sunday night that the prosecutor's office in the southern part of Sanaa had completed its interrogation of the suspect and "it was decided to try him on Monday at the court for emergency matters at the court of appeal".
A security official said he believed the assailant was insane. Yemeni television on Sunday night quoted investigation sources as saying the man was schizophrenic.
